[Title]: "Speech, 1951 July 7-12, introduction by Carrie C. Sims of the Third Episcopal District discussing signs of hope"
[Transcript]: "INTRODUCTION
Our world today is in the throes of despair. Hope for peace seems dim. What about it all? Is there really anything left in the way of hope for a bewildered world? As each day fades into the past, hundreds are being dashed into eternity by the ghastly practices of war. Bonds of human affection are bring broken - hearts are cry ng out for something abiding - for a source of assurance. Often it is out of such ti es that new hope is born. New life can spring up in the midst of despair.
Perhaps the greatest sign of hope in our perplexing age is that fellowship with Christ which gives us a sense of victory. The Cross brings a larger freedom of that fellowship. The power of the Cross fills the blackest night with the Star of universal hope - the Light of the world. The Sign of Hop?-was born in the heart of God. It is written indelibly in the Blood of the Son of God. It is sustained by His matchless love and is kept glowing by His compassion for humanity. It’s motivating qualities are love, truth, grace, mercy, and peace. The Cross is a SIGN OF HOPE to all classes - all times - all climes, and all conditions. It comforts millions - it is the only HOPE FOR A WORM IN DESPAIR.
Under the banner of the Cross will march earth’s greatest army. Though now the world is crushed into a sob, the power of the Cross will turn it into a song.
The wads of our dear Saviour come down to us through the centuries: *In the world ye shall have tribulations but be of good cheer, for I have overcome the world.” Our day needs this tonic of Hope. The future is as bright as the
promises of God.
Carrie C. Sims
Third Eplscoi>al District"

[Title]: "Speech, 1951 July 7-12, memoriam for departed missionaries"
[Transcript]: "IN MEMCRIAM
'’'The sleep of a laboring nan is sweet." Ecclesiastes 5:12.
The practice of living is a fine art, not merely a conformity to schedule. A really beautiful life is simply a good heart being natural.
The charm of life is not mechanical.
The art of fine living finds its finest expression in making others happy, and we will be remembered by what we were and the things we did. We should all have as our purpose—to leave the world better than we found it
The ministration and service of our departed workers have been varied and those who have engaged in the active mission work of our Church and the world have had consecrated hearts filled with the spirit of Christ. We honor them in our hearts and pay every tribute to their memory.
We know their brows have been wet with honest sweat. "He who attempts something and does it. well earns a night's repose.”
Today we honor and revere the departed laborers who smile on us from a heavenly rest. We can but moan the suffering and dying of our loved ones on the battle front and pray for the perfect peace which comes only when we love and trust ore another. Peace on earth comes only to men of good will.
"Forgetting ourselves, may we take our stand in close proximity to Thy cross, from whence radiate altruistic love and self-forgetting service.""

[Title]: "Letter, 1954 September 29, D. Ward Nichols to "Friends" responding to personal attacks by Dr. Hill, message"
[Transcript]: "Office of the Bishop 716 S. 19th Street Philadelphia 46, Pa.
September 29, 1954
Dear Friends:
Because of the two recent attacks of Dr. Hill upon me and because of the fact that he is not only trying his case in the Newspaper and also by circular letter, I am sending the enclosed letter that you might understand my position.
It is regrettable to say the least that a supposedly intelligent man would seek to give the Church such adverse publicity. No man with good intentions would write an open letter to the Council and then publish the same before the Council could even receive his communication. Decency would have demanded that the letter not be made public pending its receipt by the persons or person involved.
I am at a loss to know where Dr. Hill got his information that
I at any time ever made a demand on him for a public apology. This I emphatically state I have never done. I also state that I have never had so much as a brief argument with Dr. Hill. My only request was for the dismissal of a Miss Bailey whose presence I deemed against the best interest of Wilburforce University. This I had a perfect right to do as a member of the Teacher's Committee of the Trustee Board. For what purpose is a Teacher’s Committee if it does not pass upon the fitness of teachers?
When the Executive Board complied with my request I informed Bishop Allen that I would ask the Conference Treasurers to mail him the checks which they were holding. Before I could return to New York came Dr. Hill’s blast. The record will show Dr. Hill to be the worst President in the history of Wilburforce University and my prediction is that he will have resigned before you receive this letter or shortly after you receive it which proves that he selected me as an excuse for his failure and is using an imaginary conflict with me as an excuse for him to get out of a bad situation.
Please read my enclosed letter carefully.
Since 1948-49, I have paid Wilberforce University $164,010.00, which does not include another $60,000.00, which was given to Payne Seminary, making our total $224,010.00. This was just so much money wasted under the extravagant and careless administration of Dr. Hill.
I will now proceed to ask for an accounting of these funds.
Sincerely,
D. WARD NICHOLS"

[Title]: "Letter, 1954 September 29, D. Ward Nichols to "Friends" responding to personal attacks by Dr. Hill, enclosure page 1"
[Transcript]: "£^ce
REPLY OF BISHOP D. WARD NICHOLS TO THE OPEN LETTER OF DR. HILL
To state that I am amazed at the open letter to the Bishops' Council by Dr. Charles Hill of Wilberforce University expresses my feeling mildly. I have always thought that Dr. Hill, tho' eccentric, petty and "ineffective" as he stated in his letter, was truthful to say the least.
It is with considerable regret that I find it necessary to answer the vicious open letter written to the Press by Wilberforce President, Charles Hill. The Fathers of the African Methodist Episcopal Church have set up certain channels for the airing of grievances and the trying of a case in the Newspaper is not the way.
In the first place, any statement that I am holding funds belonging to Wilberforce University is entirely untrue. The funds to which Dr. Hill referred to have been turned over to the treasurer of each Annual Conference which contributed the money. I wish to call attention to the fact that funds cannot be withheld when they are given voluntarily. There is no law that calls for me to raise any amount for Wilberforce University annually. The $30,000.00 which we have contributed annually is wholly a pledge agreed upon by me and which I volunteered to raise. Any impression that I am bound to raise the $30,000.00 is incorrect.
With regard to the $8,000.00 in question, I informed Bishop Allen, chairman of the Trustee Board of Wilberforce University, as we talked in the Conrad Hilton Hotel in Chicago during the month of August, that I had returned the checks in question to the various Conference Treasurers and that I would contact the Treasurers and have the checks forwarded to the University since my request to dispense with the services of Miss Bailey was complied with.
(Photostatic copies of checks enclosed)
I felt that the Miss Bailey in question was not the type or kind of teacher that should be employed at Wilberforce University. I did not demand but I requested her dismissal by the President. This he did not see fit to do. There was never an argument nor an unkind word between the President and myself. When the news of some disagreement appeared in the Press, I was further amazed that the facts should be so distorted. Dr. Hill disclaimed any knowledge of these distorted facts - but the situation now proves that he was at all times familiar with the misinformation given to the Public.
Dr. Hill has deliberately attempted to make the Public believe that I am holding funds belonging to Wilberforce University. This is foreign to the truth. Dr. Hill is insincere in his efforts to secure the full budget which I volunteered to raise. Had he been sincere in his efforts to collect this money he would have requested of the Trustee Board (whose duties are concerned with the financial affairs of the Institution) to make this request or he could have asked the Executive Board to make this request or could have asked the Executive Board to make this request of the Bishops’ Council, my superior in all things ecclesiastical.
The fact that Dr. Hill sends an open letter to the Council shows that he had other motives than simply the collection of $8,000.00.
When I requested the dismissal of Miss Bailey, not withstanding the fact that I am a member of the Trustee Board and a member of the Teachers’ Committee of the Board whose duty it is to pass upon the fitness of teachers, he accuses me with interfering with the academic life of the University. If this is the case, by what authority does the President venture into the financial field which is wholly the prerogative of the Trustee Board. The fact is Dr. Hill has no authority to demand any money from anybody for Wilberforce University. If any demand is to be made it should come through the President of the Board or through the Board itself.
I call attention to the fact that Wilberforce University never in its history received $30,000.00 annually from the First District until I volunteered to raise the same. The record shows that the four years prior to my serving this District, Wilberforce University received $57,358.42. In the year 1947, it received only $413.89. In 1944, it received $10,007.28; in 1945, it received $9,082.00; in 1946, it received $9,235.00; in 1947, it received $413.89 and in 1948, it received $28,620.25.
During my tenure as Bishop of this Area, Wilberforce University received $162,010.00 plus $60,000.00 which Payne Seminary received, making a total of $222,010.00.
What are the facts behind the attack of Dr. Hill upon me?
1.	Dr. Hill needs a scape-goat. He thinks that I am the most likely person to be used.
2.	He has miserably failed as President of Wilberforce University. The record will show that the student body was around 600 when he assumed the presidency; it has decreased each year until it now stands at approximately 200 students.
3.	Wilberforce University is morally, spiritually and financially bankrupt. Not because the ecclesiastical politics to which Dr. Hill referred but because of his lethargy, poor leadership and lack of executive ability."

[Title]: "Letter, 1954 September 29, D. Ward Nichols to "Friends" responding to personal attacks by Dr. Hill, enclosure page 2"
[Transcript]: "4.	The debt of Wilberforce University has constantly mounted. At one time the debt was reduced to about $30,000.00 and now the indebtedness of Wilberforce is more than $100,000.00. Did my withholding $8,000 send the debt up to more than $100,000? Did my withholding $8,000 cause them to borrow thousands of dollars every year? Did my withholding $8,000 in any way cause the President to show so little concern for the financial affairs of the University that today he does not know what it costs to operate Wilberforce?
5.	Dr. Hill is wasteful, uneconomical and unintelligent concerning things financial. Admittedly, he is a great scholar but he lives in the clouds and is completely oblivious to things surrounding him. He is the best example of the combination of a great scholar and an inefficient executive that I know.
6.	Dr. Hill is not the President of Wilberforce University but the tool of certain people whom whom he takes dictation. These people, for years have lived off of Wilberforce University at the expense of the poor African Methodists and their friends who raise the money to support the institution.
7.	Dr. Hill needs a scapegoat because he is President of Wilberforce University only because he is unable to secure another position that would allow him to be as wasteful as he is in his present position. The main reason for his attack on me is not the $8,000 but the fact that he failed in his effort to be appointed Governor of the Virgin Islands. He has blamed this on his so-called enemies "on the State side" and me.
8.	Dr. Hill is wise enough to know that he has been and is a miserable failure. He sees calamity approaching and he desires to put the blame on somebody. With less than 200 students and a freshman class this year of 65 students, he sees the "handwriting on the wall".
9.	People are refusing to send their children to Wilberforce University because they see no hope of accreditation under Dr. Hill. To the North Central Association, he is a be-whiskered joke. If the President spent more time securing students and seeking accreditation, he would have less time to write slanderous articles.
10.	Oh! about Miss Bailey. I never demanded her dismissal, I simply requested her dismissal. I hold no grudge against the President in his fight to retain Miss Bailey. Under the conditions, I would have done the same thing myself.
11.	The conditions of Wilberforce can best be described as cancerous. The malignant tumor itself is the President.
12.	Dr. Hill, listening to his "Master’s" voice, timed his news release and his scandalous letters to interfere and hurt the meeting of the First Episcopal District in New York City at Bethel Church, September 29th, 30th and October 1st. Let’s see whether he succeeds or not.
13.	With all of Dr. Hill's cry about the demands which I have made, I have never made one demand of him in my life. Bishop Allen informed me that in stating to Dr. Hill my suggestion that he should let the public know the truth that an unkind word was never spoken between us and that Miss Bailey was no longer at the University, stated to me that he had never said to Dr. Hill that I was making any demand for anything. The first time that I knew of any demands that I was supposed to have made was when Dr. Hill, through the Press, accused me of making these demands. These untruths were manufactured by the President - still listening to his "Master's" voice. To make this a little more plain for the philosopher - his earthly master, made of flesh and blood, living at Wilberforce.
14.	It is lamentable that I have been compelled to state these facts for I have always sought not to try a case in the Newspaper and have always felt that any matter within the Church could be adjusted by conferences and consultation. I firmly believe that nothing can be accomplished by airing what should be family differences in public. As a firm believer in this, I have constantly refrained from answering the first attack on me by Dr. Hill in a letter which I read in the Newspaper before I received it in the mail; and the second attack which I read in the Newspaper before I received the communication as a member of the Bishops' Council.
There are other matters to which I can refer in this instance but with the interest of the Church at heart, I will hold them in abeyance pending further developments.
I think however, that my dear Brother Hill having fired his parting shot either has another job clinched or he sees the opportunity of securing one. I predict that before long my fellow Trustees at Wilberforce University will be faced with the great problem of finding a new President. In this endeavor I shall join with them in shedding tears for the passing of our lamented President and smile at the opportunity of giving to our great Wilberforce a new lease on life. It is too bad, however, that in his demise he has done this injustice to this great African Methodist heritage. The injury which he has attempted to inflict upon one of the supporters of Wilberforce will be to his everlasting discredit.
Not withstanding this parting blow, Wilberforce, her children and African Methodism in general will arise again and glory in her future triumphs."

Bear Mr, Adams:
I am the wife of John Williamson, who is at present a prisoner at the Federal Penitentiary in Lewisburg, Pa., and. I am writing to you in the hope that after you read a few simple facts in connection with his present status that you would be willing to do just one small thing in connection with it.
I will not go into a discussion of the case itself. My husband was one of the 11 Communist leaders convicted under the Smith Act and sentenced to serve five years in a federal penitentiary. In addition, he had been arrested in February 1948 for deportation to Scotland. His first application for parole was denied in February 1953 even though at that time he stated that, in view of the fact that his order for deportation had been finalized by the Immigration and Naturalization Service (while he was in jail), he would leave the country immediately if granted parole.
When his application for parole came up for recommendation in February of this year, it was again denied. However, parole can be recommended at any time.
It matters little whether you agree or disagree with the political opinions of my husband. But you might ask yourself, "What ends of justice are being served by keeping him in jail when he states that he will accept immediate departure if granted parole at this time?"
Whether you feel that he has served enough time; whether you feel that for purely humanitarian reasons he should be reunited with his family (we have two young children); whether you feel the fact that he will accept immediate departure at this time is important; it is not for me to say which of these reasons you should apply to his case. I merely want to urge that you write a letter within the next few days to the Parole Board, Dept, of Justice, Washington, D.C., asking them to grant parole to John Williamson for departure to Scotland.
I would appreciate your dropping me a line if you send such a letter, and if possible, to enclose a copy of the letter. Thanking you for your kind attention, I am,
Sincerely yours,
P.S. Any small contribution you could make to help defray the cost of these letters would be gratefully appreciated."

RELIGIOUS BELIEF IN AMERICA
CHURCH membership in the United States in 1950 (the last year for which a complete report is available) was the highest ever reported, about fifty-seven per cent of the total population. More than eighty-five million persons were members of over two hundred religious bodies which varied in belief from ultramodernist to ultrafundamentalist. Not many persons recognize the wide variety of religious thought in America today, but the accompanying chart compares the varying beliefs of America’s religious bodies.
This information was gathered through the kindness of officials of each denomination who generally responded promptly and courteously to a questionnaire about their belief. The questions that were asked are listed below, together with the total replies to each question. On following pages each religious body is listed separately. An asterisk [*] marks the ones from which no reply was received. Reference works and encyclopedic sources had to be consulted for information on these. No attempt has been made to interpret or evaluate the relative merits or demerits of various doctrines. The sole purpose has been to report on actual beliefs. Thus, though simplified, an over-all picture is presented of some of the doctrinal differences in America.
Where neither a “Yes” nor “No” answer is given it may be that (1) the information was not available, (2) a “Yes” or “No” answer would misrepresent the body’s belief,
or (3) it does not have a definite doctrine on this point.
Some organizations place emphasis on doctrine, others on the individual. Some have no creed at all, others a specific set of doctrines. [Title]: "Article, 1957 May 1, "Hospital construction Needs Resurveyed for Federal Funds""
[Transcript]: "Hospital Construction Needs Resurveyed for Federal Funds
By ROBERT V. ACKERMAN
A re-survey of hospital construction needs and possibilities in South Carolina has been completed by the State Board of Health under terms of the federal Hill-Burton Act, it was announced Tuesday.
The act provides for federal funds to match local funds on a dollar-for-dollar basis for hospital construction for various kinds of hospital facilities.
Both non-profit organizations and local government units which qualify may apply for the federal money as their own local funds become available. Formulas on a basis of population have been prepared to determine eligibility for federal matching funds.
STATE CANCER HOME
The new and latest survey figures of the State Board of Health calls for a state program of 50 beds for a State Cancer Nursing Home. The state is entitled under a systern of entitlement to have 4.600 nursing home beds. The rest of the beds not programmed are to be pooled.
For chronic diseases, with a possible authorization and entitlement of 4,606 beds, 100 beds have been programmed to the South Carolina Convalescent Home for Crippled Children at Florence, a state-wide facility and the remaining beds have been placed in a pool.
TUBERCULOSIS BEDS
Out of an entitlement of 1,409 beds to take care of tuberculosis patients 532 new beds are authorized. There are already 877 existing acceptable beds for tuberculosis patients in/ South Carolina.
In the mental health category, South Carolina is authorized 11,-515 beds. There are 2,084 existing acceptable beds in the state, the net additional number of beds which may be constructed from local funds and matching federal funds is 9,431 beds.
Authorization is available for one main public health center in each of the 46 counties of the^tate provided state funds are available for the federal matching money.
REHABILITATION NEEDS'
In the rehabilitation category South Carolina could be allotted" funds for up to eight facilities.
According to the State Board of Health, “Surveys conducted by the State Agency (Board) show that a rehabilitation center -having an integrated program as defined by federal regulations does not exist in South Carolina.”
Because of the need for highly trained and specialized personnel as well as equipment first preference in programming of matching federal funds has been given by the State Board to the Medical College Teaching Hospital at Charleston with additional units being programmed to each of the four base areas. Three other rehabilitation centers have been “held in reserve for programming as the
need for them is demonstrated.”
OUT-PATIENT CENTERS
As only 12 hospitals in South Carolina have organized out-patients departments, only seven of them classified as acceptable as far as their plant is concerned, the State Board has programmed to ensure at least one center in, every hospital area.
The formula for matching funds would allow South Carolina to have 230 of these centers.
In addition mental health centers have been programmed for Columbia, Charleston, Spartanburg, Greenville, Florence and Anderson while on a state-wide basis centers have been programmed for the Medical College -Out-patient Department in Charleston and the South Carolina Sanatorium (TB) in Columbia. The remaining mental health centers have been pooled for distribution as the need for them is demonstrated. J
The South Carolina State Board of Health, designated as the sole state agency in the state,, developed the detailed regulations prescribed by the Surgeon General of the U.S. Public Health Service.
The South Carolina Hospital Ad-visory^Council, the Executive Committee of the State Board of Health, and the U. S. Public Health Service shared their advice on the programming of the matching funds.
These federal funds are not available unless local public or private, agencies apply, qualify and provide local funds"

A Mutual Insurance Company
3100 West Lake Street • Minneapolis 16, Minnesota
July 22, 1957
Dr. E. A. Adams
2113 Lady Street
Columbia 16, South Carolina
Dear Dr. Adams:
May I take the liberty of asking you for some information of an historical nature about the African Msthodist Episcopal Church? According to the year book of the National Council of Churches you are the historiographer of the denomination and may be able to answer our questions. Dorothy Johnson Latimer, who is a correspondent in our office and comes from Columbia, knows you and believes that it is possible you can be of assistance.
Our company, as you probably know, insures clergymen of all denominations. For some years we have included in our quarterly bulletin to members pictures of historic churches in different parts of the country, usually with a brief text descriptive of the historical interest and specific architectural features that might be worthy of note.
Earlier this year when I was in Philadelphia I was informed that the oldest church of the A.M.E. is in that city. It is known as "Old Mother Bethel," the congregation being formed by Richard Allen in 1797 and the building dedicated at a somewhat later date by Bishop Asbury. I hope these facts are correct and that the building is still standing. I did not have an opportunity to see it.
Do you have available a brief historical sketch of this building that we could borrow or have a copy of? If so we would appreciate the use of this information to get the facts straight.
Then we would like to have a photograph, glossy, at least 5x7" and of professional rather than "snapshot" quality. We would prefer to pay for such a picture so that we could keep it permanently in our file, and if necessary could arrange to have a suitable photograph taken. And in that case we certainly would see that you would have a copy of the picture for your files.
Oakley R. Tripp, President • Andrew Hobart, Vice-President, Secretary • David F. Hobart, Treasurer • Rev. William J. Bell, D. D., Chairman"

[Title]: "Article, 1957 August 17, "Allen University Board Over-rides President; Retains Three Professors""
[Transcript]: "SATURDAY, AUGUST 17, 1W
Fo Save Drowning Woman
Allen University Board Over-rides President; Retains Three Professors
Special to Journal and Guide
COLUMBIA, S. C. — By unanimous vote, the Board of Control and the Executive Committee of the Board of Trustees of Alien university here over-rode a demand by President Frank R. Veal that three professors be made to resign or be fired. The vote came after a day-long session Aug. 6.
Retained by the Board were Dr. Edwin D. Hoffman, chairman of the division of education; Dr. John Granville Rideout, chairman of the division of humanities; and Dr. Forrest Oran Wiggins who teaches in the latter division. Hoffman and Rideout are white.
THE DAILY PRESS report ed in a prominently-placed article on the morning of the meeting that Rideout and Wiggins were both outstanding in the Progressive Party in 1948 and that they had lost posts at other institutions because of their liberal beliefs.
In addition it was played up that Dr. Rideout had at one time signed a petition calling for a “cease fire in Korea.” On this point one board member declared, “I suppose Veal would like to impeach Pres. Eisenhower for being elected on a landslide by promising to
stop the fighting in Korea and bring the boys home. Eisenhower would have needed ■ cease fire to do that.
The three retained professors were gratified by the action of the board. They joined in a statement that they enjoy serving at Allen and hope to continue there as long as th# board of trustees is pleased with their work.
Allen University, supported by the African Methodist Episcopal church, boasts an enrollment of approximately 1,000 students, and is named for Richard Allen the first bishop of the church.
PRESIDENT VEAL did not recommend to the board that the men be dismissed, despite earlier demands and threats. He presented no charges, and on being asked pointedly by Bishop -I. H. Benner, chancellor of the university, presiding, whether the president’s report meant that he was recommending that all faculty members are to be re-elected, he admitted that this was true.
Despite endorsement of the three professors by the board, President Veal in interviews with the white press insisted that his earlier request for the resignations of the three men means that they now have one year’s notice of dismissal.
IN CONTRAST Bishop Bonner said in a statement to the press that none of the three could be dismissed without the
approval of the board.
Observers expressed themselves openly as being highly incensed by persistent reports over a long period that Pres
Veal had submitted to pressures exerted by Dixiecrat officials who sought to dictate who should teach at Allen.
That the college head may have capitulated to forces opposed to full citizenship rights for Negroes in South .Carolina is borne out by other reports that he has carried out demands that he delete mention
of the NAACP youth council
from the new college catalog."

[Title]: "Brochure, no date, information on the South Carolina Council on Human Relations, interior"
[Transcript]: "South Carolina Council on Human Relations
1508 LADY STREET	COLUMBIA, S. C.
An organization of Southerners of both races working together in the interest of all the people of South Carolina
SOUTH CAROLINA IS TRADITIONALLY A state the blandness of whose climate is matched by the courtesy and neighborliness of its people. In recent years, however, the summers have been growing hotter and the tempers of the people shorter. Why?
We can omit the weather since we’re not going to do anything about it; but we are the people, and we can profitably ask, what is happening to us?
Courtesy and neighborliness, though fundamental things, are fragile. Civilized, not barbaric virtues. They grow in a certain climate of opinion. They are the fruit of peace, not conflict.
TODAY THERE ARE SHARP DIFFERENCES of opinion among the citizens of South Carolina. The decision of the Supreme Court in regard to segregation has challenged an established custom, and citizens differ as to the course of action to pursue. The threatened breakdown of any custom disturbs a traditional society, and in the disturbance other customs are endangered. Especially such civilized customs as courtesy and neighborliness.
YET ALL THOUGHTFUL SOUTH CAROLINIANS, white and Negroes, agree that regardless of our differences on the issue of segregation, we must preserve our traditional and civilized virtues of courtesy and neighborliness. But how preserve them? How defend such fragile things?
THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS IS THE BEST ANSWER.
WHAT IS THE COUNCIL? Its history is long and honorable. It originated in the troubled days of 1919 as the South Carolina Committee of the Commission on Interracial cooperation. It be
came, in 1943, the South Carolina Division of the Southern Regional Council, and, in 1954, the South Carolina Council on Human Relations. It is an affiliate of the Southern Regional Council, of Atlanta. Its membership is unrestricted as to race or creed. It aims at a better life for all South Carolinians. If the racial issue concerns it most at present, that is because the racial issue concerns South Carolinians most at present.
WHAT DOES THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS PROPOSE TO DO ABOUT THIS PROBLEM? In the first place, it has no final answer. That answer lies with the people, and with time, and will change as people change and time passes. The South Carolina Council on Human Relations proposes merely to make the problem easier of solution by calling into full play the traditional virtues of courtesy and neighborliness. Relying upon these accepted values, South Carolinians will cooperate to solve the problem which now seems so difficult.
HOW DOES THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS PROPOSE TO DO THIS? By using its influence, through its paid staff and through its membership, to persuade the leading citizens, white and Negro, of individual South Carolina Communities to confer and consider their problems; to give authoritative information and professional service when requested; and to keep such groups, and all others which may be interested, informed as to the progress of interracial understanding and cooperation in the South.
WHAT ARE THE RESOURCES OF THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS? First, and most important, the
respect and trust which this organization and its affiliate, the Southern Regional Council, composed of Southerners working for the South, have won in the South through years of service. Second, a paid professional staff, composed of an executive director, an associate executive director, and an office secretary; third, professional studies on the problems of the South, financed and guided by the Southern Regional Council, and available from that organization.
WHAT DOES THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS NEED? The support, both financial and moral, of all South Carolinians who believe that we have, within our hearts and customs, the resources for solving even the difficult problems of today. The Council can serve only as the instrument for clarifying and organizing this strength. The strength is in South Carolinians, native to US, as much a part of us as the landscape through which we move.
But the organization of these resources takes money. Fortunately, this year the salaries of the South Carolina Council’s staff will be paid through the Southern Regional Council. However, all operating expenses must be raised by the South Carolina Council. These funds will come from both memberships and contributions. All contributions are tax-exempt. The several types of membership are listed below.
FINALLY. No matter how problems arise, they are settled at last only by the people involved; our school problems by all the citizens of the many communities of South Carolina. In a democratic society like ours, this means through the representative citizens, white and Negro, of each community. All-white groups and all-Negro groups may have their part to play; but the matter will be finally settled only by white and Negroes conferring together in the give-and-take of the democratic process.
THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS IS THE ONE ORGANIZATION in the State today whose purpose it is to exemplify the method which will be used. It therefore unhesitatingly asks the support of all South Carolinians who cherish for their State a future even more splendid than its nast"

TO MEMBERS OF THE TRUSTEE BOARD, MINISTERS, LAYMEN, ALUMNI AND FRIENDS
This no doubt will be my last written communication to you before the day of election. I have tried in previous communications to present my case to you representing my interest in serving you as president of Allen University. Some of you I have had the opportunity of coming into your homes for a fireside chat, for this fellowship I am very grateful to you. It is with much regret that I was not able to visit all of you, but being so engrossed with the responsibility assigned to me as a member of the committee appointed to run Allen University during the interim of electing a president, I was unable to leave the university for any length of time. I trust that you will not take it as an offense or as a selective oversight on my part.
Soon you will be called to attend a board meeting at which time no doubt the election of the president of Allen University will take place. Their images are looking down upon you this day and their spirits are gathering on the banks of glory watching you their sons and daughters with hopes that you will prove worthy of the heritage transcended to you. [Title]: "Brochure, 1953, Sumter National Farm Loan Association 1953 Annual Report to Shareholders, page 2-3"
[Transcript]: "FACTS ABOUT THE "Farmer Owned" LAND BANK SYSTEM
1.	THE COOPERATIVE LAND BANK SYSTEM is composed of the 12 Federal Land Banks and about 1200 National Farm Loan Associations, with assets of over one billion dollars.
2.	THE NATIONAL FARM LOAN ASSOCIATIONS own all of the capital of the Federal Land Banks and all the capital of the National Farm Loan Associations is owned by their farmer members.
3.	THE LAND BANK SYSTEM is self-supporting and all operating expenses including supervision and examination are paid from earnings of the Banks and the Associations.
4.	FUNDS FOR LENDING OPERATIONS are obtained thru the sale of Bonds to the investing public. These Bonds are joint obligations of the 12 Federal Land Banks and are not guaranteed by the Government either as to principal or in-terest.
5.	LENDING Operations are conducted through the National Farm Loan Associations. All loans must be approved by the local Association before they can be made by the Land Bank.
6.	THE 72 NATIONAL FARM LOAN ASSOCIATIONS in Florida, Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina handle all loans for the Columbia Land Bank in these states.
COOPERATIVE CREDIT SERVICES AVAILABLE TO FARMERS
1.	PURPOSES OF LOANS.
Among the purposes for which loans may be made are:
(a)	Purchase of land for agricultural uses.
(b)	Purchase of equipment, livestock, etc.
(c)	Erect or repair buildings and for land improvement, including forest land.
(d)	Pay indebtedness and provide funds for general agricultural uses.
(e)	For any agricultural purpose or needs related to the farmer and his family.
2.	BASIS OF LOANS.
Loans are based on the normal agricultural value of the farm including the value of forest land. The normal income from the farm is a principal factor in determining the normal value.
3.	LOAN TERMS.
Loans may be made for terms of 5 to 40 years. Payments of principal and interest may be made either annually or semi-annually. Adjustments in the repayment schedule may be made to meet changes in local agricultural conditions.
4.	APPLICATIONS FOR LOANS are made to the Secretary-Treasurer of the National Farm Loan Association serving the county in which the farm offered as security is located.
5.	THE LOCAL NATIONAL FARM LOAN ASSOCIATION handles the making and servicing of all loans for the Columbia Land Bank in its chartered territory.
6.	ALL REQUESTS for information should be sent to the local Association at the address given in this circular."

[Title]: "Letter, 1950 February 14, Adams to the members of the Board of Education of the A.M.E. Church presenting a quadrennial report"
[Transcript]: "Jacksonville, Fla. February 14, 1950
Bishop L. H. Hemingway, Members of the Board of Education of the African Methodist Episcopal Church,5 arid ^l^^	-.
Visiting Friends:	■	'
It is with pleasure that I render my second report for this quadrennium. I am very pl-eased to have such an a^Jky of distinguished churchmen as members of this Board."0^' (Distinguished chairman is showing his worth to the great church of his choice by the service he is rendering to the same.
The educational system of the nation and many of the states, is being revamped and the standards are being formulated and raised. Added to this, the removal of almost all’ of the Bishops from the districts over which they formerly *, presided, has made readjustments very necessary.
A program of expansion is being fostered in every school in the church. Many of them have large building programs. Some of them are having serious trouble in meeting the financial needs. Others are moving along very successfully on a pay as you go basis. Whatever may be the circumstances, there should be no question as to our maintaining our church affiliated schools. All other denominations are maintaining and improving their colleges and I am sure that the great African Methodist Episcopal Church will not be found wanting.
The schools to which -the Department of Education has made contributions this fiscal year are: Wilberforce Uni-versity, Wilberforce, Ohio; Allen University, Columbia, S. C.; Morris Brown College, Atlanta, Ga.; Edward Waters College, Jacksonville, Fla.; Paul Quinn College, Waco, Tex.; Campbell College, Jackson, Miss.; Daniel Payne College, Birmingham, Ala.; Shorter College, Little Rock, Ark.; Payne Theological Seminary, Wilberforce, Ohio; and the Nurses Training School at Western University, Kansas City, Kan. Kittrell College, Kittrell, N. C., is going through a stage of needed repairs and will soon take her place with the other schools of the church.

[Title]: "Letter, 1950 March 11, President T.B. Jones of Harbison Junior College to ""Friends"" thanking them for contributions to the Founder's Day Program"
[Transcript]: "83$f
Harbison Junior College Irmo, South Carolina March 11, 1950
Dear Friends:
The Founder’s Day Program was excellent and the formal effort loomed reasonably large, thanks to your interest and support.
You will be interested to know that the Rev. Moses S. Belton, Registrar of Johnson C. Smith University, and Mrs. Charity Nash Adams, of Columbia, South Carolina, were the principal speakers of the Founder’s Day exercises. Mrs. Adams rehearsed for the audience reflections of Old Harbison days; while Mr. Belton estimated values of the current program and then took a brief look at what the future seems to offer Harbison of Tomorrow.
The degree to which Harbison Junior College can and shall effectively leave her imprint in the several communities and states which the students now represent shall depend not only upon the clarity with which present day problems of society are understood here on the campus, but also upon the effectiveness with which Harbison students of years gone by persist in blazing trails of glory for the way of life which the Institution has endeavored to instill in all who have trod these grounds.
Your efforts as exhibited by your contributions this year shall be recounted and appreciated by the many yet to come, as well as by those now enrolled at Harbison.
The contributions on Founder's Day represented a large number: The staff and students gave personally a fair sum, their immediate friends also responded to the effort quite well. The Alumni and former students, and friends, however, are they whose efforts made the annual rally a success.
Whereas the total results of our Founder’s Day Rally netted slightly more than $800.00, the Alumni, former students and friends contributed nearly $450.00 of that sum*
To each and every one whose contribution, efforts end good wishes made the Dey a success, I wish to say "Thank You" for •very Herblsantes.
Sincerely yours,
T. B. Jones
President"

Dear Pastor and Friend:
Subject: "SUNDAY MAY 23, A SPECIAL DAY OF PRAYER"
Our faith in God prompts us to feel moved to have a special day of thanksgiving at this hour when the Supreme Court has answered the challenge and call of democracy in handing down the decision making segregation in public schools unconstitutional.
Certainly with all African Methodists having worked and prayed toward this great objective, we can not help but feel that God has smiled upon our nation, the Supreme Court and upon all of us in this historic hour in which righteousness and truth have triumphed.
Therefore, as Presiding bishop of the Seventh Episoo pal District of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, I decree Sunday May 23rd as a Special Day of Prayer at which time prayers will be offered in all of our churches and homes thanking God for the Supreme Court and its decision, thanking God for our nation and the Democractic way of life, also praying that God will grant guidance to our leaders and our people in working together most calmly in making the recognition of the law an easy matter here in South Carolina and in our nation,,

August 29, 1956
Reverend and dear Sir:
The Negro Minister has at this time a gr ater opportunity than he has had since reconstruction days to advance his people po litically.
Working together in support of the Republican ticket in the November general election, we will help vouchsafe the gains in "Civil Rights” that have been made under the Eisenhower administration, and furthermore, we can help bring back the two party system in South Carolina.
You are no doubt familiar with the factional disputes that have been carried on in Republican politics in this State. Well, the answer to the question of who is the right Republican group in South Carolina was given by the National G. 0. P convention just held in the Cow Palace, San Mateo County, California.
The group that was recognized and duly seated in the National Convention was known as the "Dews Faction". It is now "The Republican Party of South Carolina" and it is under its auspices that we are working and to which you are hereby Invited to identify yourself if you have not already done so. The delegation of the erstwhile "Dows Group" included four Negroes, and four others were included in the convention staff as paid workers. This is in sharp contrast to the South Carolina Democratic delegation ih Chicago. They did’nt have a place for a single Negro, and absolutely refused to make a place for a single,solitary one.
A strong Republican party is soon to be built in South Carolina. Let us give to this much needed second party the weight of our moral influence and support. There are hundreds of jobs in this State that are controlled by federal patronage, such as Judgeships,Post Masterships, rural letter carriers, positions as U. S. Marshalls, Deputy U. S. Marshalls, census takers, etc. If Negroes in this State join the Republican party in large enough numbers and deliver a strong vote for the G.O.P in. November, they will have much to gain, and will have some sayso as to who will get these jobs."

BARITONE AND TENOR SOLI WITH CHORUS “FATHER FORGIVE THEM, FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.”
Then cried out the people. He of death is guilty, Take Him, Take Him, let us crucify Him; let His blood be on us and on our children.
Then crucified they Jesus and the two thieves, one on His right hand and the other one on His left hand.
Second Word
DUET FOR TENOR AND BARITONE WITH CHORUS “VERILY, THOU TO-DAY, SHALT BE WITH ME IN PARADISE, AMEN, SO I TELL THEE.”
0 Lord remember me, when Thou comest into Thy kingdom.
Third Word
SOLI FOR SOPRANO, TENOR, BARITONE, WITH CHORUS
“WOMAN, BEHOLD THY SON.”
See the holy mother sighing,
Watches as her son is dying,
Bleeding on the cruel cross.
Who could see her without weeping,
As she kneeleth vigil keeping,
Bowed by her grief and fearful loss?
Fourth Word
BARITONE SOLO
“0 MY FATHER WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?”
All those who were my friends have now forsaken me, and they that hate me have risen up against me, and they have all betrayed me whom I loved.
Even the vine that once I planted and that oft I tended: why has all thy sweetness more and more turned to bitterness, that thou dost crucify me?
Fifth Word
CHORUS, AND SOLI FOR TENOR AND BARITONE
“I THIRST”
And the Jews then passing by Him, railed on Him and mocked Him, both wagging their heads at Him, and crying to him:
Ah Thou that wouldst destroy the temple, if Thou be Jesus, Son of the Father, now from the cross descend Thou that we may see Thee and believe Thee, when we behold it. If Thou art king over Israel save thyself now.
Sixth Word
TENOR SOLO, AND CHORUS
“FATHER, INTO THY KEEPING I COMMEND MY SOUL"
For Thou art my Father and my God, Thou art my Saviour in time of trouble.
Seventh Word
SOLID FOR SOPRANO, TENOR & BARITONE, WITH CHORUS
ONCE MORE SPAKE JESUS, CRYING WITH A LOUD VOICE:
“IT IS FINISHED!”
And Jesus bowed down His head and yielded up the ghost.
And about the sixth hour there was darkness, obscuring the sun's light, and darkness covered the earth until about the ninth hour: and the veil of the temple was rent, and the trembling earth did quake, rocks were rending, graves were opening and saints arose.
Prayer
Thee we adore, 0 Saviour Bless Thee and praise Thee for ever. For on Thy holy cross Thou hast the world from sin redeemed.
BENEDICTION—"

[Title]: "Letter, 1957 March 17, President Jeff Steinert of the S.C. Chapter of the American Association of Hospital Accountants to potential members enclosing membership applications, page 1"
[Transcript]: "American Association of Hospital Accountants
SOUTH CAROLINA CHAPTER
A review of the records of the South Carolina Chapter of AAHA reveals that your Hospital is not represented in the Association.
It is almost impossible that the Chapter's activities have not affected you. During the past year Blue Cross and the Industrial Commission have adopted a common billing form that the Chapter developed in conjunction with them. This, billing form can also be used in billing other third parties including insurance companies, as well as standardizing on a state-wide basis billings to patients. In this case, South Carolina is first in the forty-eight.
With few exceptions, all Hospitals are using the AHA (Duke) system of accounts. However, this is not a requirement of membership, and most of our present efforts are being made toward more simple and more efficient systems and procedures, and more effective use of financial and statistical information as a tool for better hospital administration.
While policy may change from Hospital to Hospital, each patient must be admitted, his account posted, and he must be discharged. All hospitals have common third parties such as the Industrial Commission, Blue Cross and insurance companies. Many hospitals bill various State agencies; all hospitals have varying degrees of difficulties in Credit and Collections. Every effort to standardize is a step toward progress, for then educational problems are simplified. Once the education problem is solved, public relations improve, because patients and third parties understand there is only one way that hospitals do business.
Our progress during the past three years could have been faster and more effective if our membership represented a higher percentage of the total number of hospitals in the State. However, the present members realize the value of the Association, and their increasing interest and participation have been responsible for the accomplishments of the past year.
This is to invite your Hospital to be in on the ground floor to help establish and improve public relations through good business procedures, to help us to standardize procedures with third parties by adding your weight to the united efforts of many other Hospitals."

[Transcript]: "Your membership, too, means assistance to you; assistance in training your Admitting, Business Office and Accounting personnel by association with others who have proven themselves capable in their fields. Our "Question Box" furnishes a means to solving actual problems. At our quarterly meetings, each of the various phases of Hospital business problems is discussed, and new and more simple procedures are discussed, published and circulated.
Enclosed is an application for membership. The dues are nominal; the results well worthwhile. Your Accountant or Business Manager can be spared four days per year to reduce his worries and help solve his problems. If you don't think so, sign your name to the application blank and come join us. The dues of most of our present members are paid by the Hospitals they represent.
Very truly yours,
President, S. C. Chapter

[Transcript]: "Why EVERY NEGRO in the WORLD Should See the Beautiful Technicolor Motion Picture
PILLARS OF THE KINGDOM
1.	It opens the UNTOLD and AMAZING Story of the New Africa.
2.	It presents the most progressive Negro-ruled country in Africa. You’ll see million-dollar hotels, banks, department stores being erected and not on a medicine-dropper scale.
3.	You’ll see the richest-endowed country in the world. Its in AFRICA! In natural resources, compared with it, California, Pennsylvania and Florida are poverty stricken.
4.	It’s the world Premiere showing the GLOBAL achievements and the historic outreach of the great AM E Zion Church.
5.	You will see in technicolor and sound, the land of the fighting Ashantis, that unsuppressible proud African race, which the British defeated, and kept under martial law for nearly 40 years but never conquered.
6.	In full colors, you’ll see in action the shrewd HAUSAS, foremost Negro Traders on earth. They’re the match of Jews, Scotch and Chinese.
7.	You’ll come face to face with Africa’s beautiful children, easily among the most unspoiled children of the world.
8.	You’ll see the most beautiful stream-lined city in ail Africa.
9.	You’ll get a peep at the new state house of LIBERIA, most striking under the sun.
10.	You’ll drive along file Marina (Mah-reen-er) in bustling, thriving Lagos, where Negroes learn, practice and operate more business than anywhere else on the globe.
11.	In this ultra rich historic movie you’ll see a product of Zion who heads the State Police and Parole Board with 10,000 under his supervision in Illinois.
12.	In Harrisburg, you’ll see another son of Zion who directs the one billion 800 million dollar budget of the state of Pennsylvania.
13.	You’ll see and hear Zion’s Bishops, choirs and others recorded in sound and colors and mannerisms so that their personalities may be preserved for posterity.
14.	The movie is designed to stimulate people to lear.i the world in which Zion works, and to have greater appreciation for religion and its service to mankind. It calls us to support our people in Africa.
15.	PILLARS OF THE KINGDOM was made with the cooperation of the Board of Bishops of the AMEZ Church under the direction of COLOR Magazine by Tri Continental Film Corporation. This is a new company coming into being to help give dignity and better treatment to Negroes and all people, and to stimulate and serve Negro life and all life in the modern world.
Be among the first 4,000 to see PILLARS OF THE KINGDOM in its World Premiere in Pittsburgh where it will be shown in cooperation with the Quadrennial Conference of the A M E Zion Church and with the cooperation of all denominations who are team-working to assist the visiting Zion Conference.

[Title]: "Letter, 1957 June 20, Mrs. Alice S. Brown to Adams requesting information about a hospital position"
[Transcript]: "1228 Heidt Street Columbia, South Carolina
June 20, 1957
The Rev. E. A. Adams
Chairman of the Board
Good Samaritan Wavely Hospital Columbia, South Carolina
Dear Sir:
I am writing you for some written information in. reply to this letter. At the present time, I am just on the Staff without any knowledge of what the future will bring in my employment. Have you in mind what a maximum salary for an Experienced Operating Room Supervisor will be? If so, do you plan to give an annual raise each year until the maximum salary is reached?
Do you consider a three weeks vacation annually for Supervisors plus accumulated time and sick leave?
You see, Rev. Adams the nursing profession is a progressive one with many fields to choose from. It is impossible for each nurse to get the same salary in the same hospital, because their duties are not the same. Nurses are paid according to positions, experience and shifts, plus time in a half, for over time. For example, when I return to the hospital for emergency operations after duty hours.
I made myself available for such duties since my employment on your staff, because I don’t think you know about it since it was such a shortage of nurses and no one else was available.
With the cost of living conditions every day and having children to support, I am asking for the given information, because I just have to supplement my present salary in some way.
I should like to call your attention to a raise that was promised to me occuring April 1, 1957? which I didn't get. I guess it was due to the change in Administraters around that time. Have you considered my vacation pay for 1956.
I will appreciate whatever consideration you have in mind, but I will appreciate some further information.
Yours very truly,
Mrs. Alice S. Brown"

[Title]: "Letter, 1958 January 8, Copy of Letter to Bishop Bonner from Allen University to members of the Board of Trustees"
[Transcript]: "We are sending you a copy of our letter to Bishop Bonner for your information as a member of the Executive Board of the Board of Trustees.
January 8, 1958 Dear Bishop Bonner:
We have searched our conscience and spent many hours in careful thought on what is best for Allen University and the people of the South.
In trying to make our decision we have considered the following questions:
1.	Why, after years of conscientious and able service to Allen, and after repeated commendation for our contribution to education at Allen, are we treated in a most unprofessional and ungrateful fashion?
2.	Why is it that to this very moment no specific reasons have been given for the request to resign? A professor d eserves to hear charges and to refute them when they are false. To ask a man to resign without giving reasons is like asking a man to sign a blank check. No honorable man can do this.
i.
3.	flow can Allen fail to challenge decertification when the state board of education has, we are advised by distinguished attorneys,' clearly exceeded its powers and can clearly have its illegal action contested in the courts? The state has violated the consti tutional rights of Allen, its students, and its professors.
4.	The state has refused to give publicly reasons for its decertification of Allen. Does not this confirm the fact that their attack is not upon us but upon Negro education?
5.	We also must ask what effect bowing to the Timmermans will have on the movement for equal rights in our country. It is certain that the Citizens1 Councils and the Ku Klux Klan will be encouraged and the fine people of Clarendon County, Orangeburg, Montgomery, Little Rock, etc. be disheartened.
6.	How can Allen University help itself by giving in to dictation from politicians whose every move is designed to degrade Negroes, and to weaken the struggle for integration. Is not the dignity and independence of Allen its most precious possession?
As you know, we have consistently kept the best interest of Allen University uppermost. Since we believe that this principle has also guided your thinking, we earnestly request that you reconsider your course of action in the light of the questions here raised. We plan to see you Friday morning as promised and to discuss the matter further.
Respectfully yours,
DR. EDWIN D. HOFFMAN
DR. JOHN G. RIDEOUT

[Title]: "Letter, 1958 January 6, Letter to the Editor from Allen University"
[Transcript]: "LETTER TO THE EDITOR
To the Editor:
2025 Marion Street Columbia, S. C. January 6, 195?
The de-certification of Allen University by the State Board of Education and the reported demand by Governor George Bell Timmerman, Jr. that Allen oust three of its most distinguished professors has become a matter of deep concern to many South Carolinians.
The gravity of the State Board's action and its potential far-reaching effects for education in South Carolina prompt me to suggest what, in my opinion, are some of the implications of this matter.
Primarily, the action of the Board, patently illegal and unconstitutional, is in clear violation of the "due process of law" and the "equal protection of the laws" provisions of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States.
In addition, the action of the Board was both arbitrary and discriminatory in that the Board held no form of hearing, presented the professors with no grounds for its action, and failed to offer either the men or the college the opportunity to be heard.
Furthermore, the Board, by its action, has interfered with the contractual relationship between employers and employees, and laid itself open to legal attack.
Obviously, one might easily conclude that the Board has esceeded its legal powers by seeking to select or to dismiss the faculty members of private colleges. Uhile it e.asily can be seen that it is within the province of the State Board of Education to determine certain general standards related to teacher certification, it is not difficult to see that the Board would be hard put to produce clearly defined standards that would allow it to dictate the composition of the faculties of private colleges in South Carolina,
Also, to all appearances, the Board has violated the constitutional guarantees on the separation of church and State for Allen is not only a private institution, but it is also a college owned and operated by a Prostestant denomination. It receives not one single penny of support from the State of South Carolina.
The Board’s pattern of action, so foreign to a democracy, has not been unusual in lands where the obvious objective was to stiffle free thinking and progressive action in order to carry out the ulterior motives of the state. Such repressive action against Allen, following fast upon the ousting of Dean Chester Travelstead from the University of South Carolina, undoubtedly has been making it almost impossible to attract distinguished educators and scholars in sufficient numbers to the schools and colleges of South Carolina.
Reports on the September 21, 1957 meeting of the State Board of Education told of a 16-page questionnaire form that was to be completed and signed by the presidents and directors of teaching education in the public and private institutions of higher learning in South Carolina."

South Carolina Council on Human Relations
1508 LADY STREET	COLUMBIA, S. C.
An organization of Southerners of both races working together in the interest of all the people of South Carolina
SOUTH CAROLINA IS TRADITIONALLY A state the blandness of whose climate is matched by the courtesy and neighborliness of its people. In recent years, however, the summers have been growing hotter and the tempers of the people shorter. Why?
We can omit the weather since we’re not going to do anything about it; but we are the people, and we can profitably ask, what is happening to us?
Courtesy and neighborliness, though fundamental things, are fragile. Civilized, not barbaric virtues. They grow in a certain climate of opinion. They are the fruit of peace, not conflict.
TODAY THERE ARE SHARP DIFFERENCES of opinion among the citizens of South Carolina. The decision of the Supreme Court in regard to segregation has challenged an established custom, and citizens differ as to the course of action to pursue. The threatened breakdown of any custom disturbs a traditional society, and in the disturbance other customs are endangered. Especially such civilized customs as courtesy and neighborliness.
YET ALL THOUGHTFUL SOUTH CARO-LINIANS, white and Negroes, agree that regardless of our differences on the issue of segregation, we must preserve our traditional and civilized virtues of courtesy and neighborliness. But how preserve them? How defend such fragile things?
THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS IS THE BEST ANSWER.
WHAT IS THE COUNCIL? Its history is long and honorable. It originated in the troubled days of 1919 as the South Carolina Committee of the Commission on Interracial cooperation. It be
came, in 1943, the South Carolina Division of the Southern Regional Council, and, in 1954, the South Carolina Council on Human Relations. It is an affiliate of the Southern Regional Council, of Atlanta. Its membership is unrestricted as to race or creed. It aims at a better life for all South Carolinians. If the racial issue concerns it most at present, that is because the racial issue concerns South Carolinians most at present.
WHAT DOES THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS PROPOSE TO DO ABOUT THIS PROBLEM? In the first place, it has no final answer. That answer lies with the people, and with time, and will change as people change and time passes. The South Carolina Council on Human Relations proposes merely to make the problem easier of solution by calling into full play the traditional virtues of courtesy and neighborliness. Relying upon these accepted values, South Carolinians will cooperate to solve the problem which now seems so difficult.
HOW DOES THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS PROPOSE TO DO THIS? By using its influence, through its paid staff and through its membership, to persuade the leading citizens, white and Negro, of individual South Carolina Communities to confer and consider their problems; to give authoritative information and professional service when requested; and to keep such groups, and all others which may be interested, informed as to the progress of interracial understanding and cooperation in the South.
WHAT ARE THE RESOURCES OF THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS? First, and most important, the
respect and trust which this organization and its affiliate, the Southern Regional Council, composed of Southerners working for the South, have won in the South through years of service. Second, a paid professional staff, composed of an executive director, an associate executive director, and an office secretary; third, professional studies on the problems of the South, financed and guided by the Southern Regional Council, and available from that organization.
WHAT DOES THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS NEED? The support, both financial and moral, of all South Carolinians who believe that we have, within our hearts and customs, the resources for solving even the difficult problems of today. The Council can serve only as the instrument for clarifying and organizing this strength. The strength is in South Carolinians, native to us, as much a part of us as the landscape through which we move.
But the organization of these resources takes money. Fortunately, this year the salaries of the South Carolina Council’s staff will be paid through the Southern Regional Council. However, all operating expenses must be raised by the South Carolina Council. These funds will come from both memberships and contributions. All contributions are tax-exempt. The several types of membership are listed below.
FINALLY. No matter how problems arise, they are settled at last only by the people involved; our school problems by all the citizens of the many communities of South Carolina. In a democratic society like ours, this means through the representative citizens, white and Negro, of each community. All-white groups and all-Negro groups may have their part to play; but the matter will be finally settled only by white and Negroes conferring together in the give-and-take of the democratic process.
THE SOUTH CAROLINA COUNCIL ON HUMAN RELATIONS IS THE ONE ORGANIZATION in the State today whose purpose it is to exemplify the method which will be used. It therefore unhesitatingly asks the support of all South Carolinians who cherish for their State a future even more splendid than its nasi-"

[Title]: "Article, 1955 August 10, "Racial Amity and Good Will Is S.C. Council's Mission" by W.D. Workman, Jr."
[Transcript]: "Racial Amity And Good Will Is S. C. Council’s Mission
By W. D. Workman, Jr.
A little organization with a big mission is seeking to bring South Carolinians around to the frame of mind that problems growing out of the Supreme Court’s anti-segregation decision can best be met by biracial amity on the local level.
The South Carolina Council on Human Relations has no specific answer or answers to the complex questions arising out of the segregation issue, but it does have the conviction that those answers necessarily will demand the best thought and action from responsible leaders of both races.
Along with that conviction seems to be the basic assumption that the state must move in the direction of compliance with the Supreme Court decision.
But even so, the Council is making no pronouncements of what should or should not be done. Its president, The Rev. J. Claude Evans, editor of the Methodist Advocate, describes himself as a “moderate” in the field of race relations and is frank to admit that he has no simple, sure solution to the problem growing out of the segregation decision.
He places his emphasis on the need for establishing more and better “communication” between the races, for finding out the facts involved in each local situation, and for making biracial studies of local involvements and possibilities.
The state executive director of the Council on Human Relations, Mrs. Alice N. Spearman, feels that the Council contributes more by stressing “processes” rather than panaceas.
, In her constant movement a., bout South Carolina, she seeks to bring existing agencies into greater cooperation with one another on questions affecting race relations.
Logically enough, her attention is primarily concerned with the
AUG 10 1955
problem of school segregation, and she is actively promoting the formation of study groups of citizens in communities where the problem is or is expected to become acute.
Only secondarily is she attempting to build up membership in the Council on Human Relations.
, Actually, there are fewer than a half-dozen local councils in the entire state. Rock Hill is the most active, for it has been stimulated by an outspoken Catholic priest, the Very Rev. Maurice Shean, and enjoys a degree of official recognition in that Mayor Em-mette Jerome is a member of the state board and has appointed a Mayor’s Committee on Human Relations.
In Anderson, the Christian Council on Human Relations is serving the same cause. In Spartanburg, the United Church Women are carrying on similar work.
Informal meeting are held elsewhere in the state, and the state Council has individual members scattered throughout South Carolina who maintain their annual $3.50 memberships or who make other contributions to the state or local work.
The South Carolina Council on Human Relations (and those of other Southern States) grew out of the Southern Regional Council.
Last year that organization, which is dedicated to “equal opportunity for all peoples in the South,” received a $240,000 grant from the Fund for the Republic.
(The Fund was established by the Ford Foundation in 1952 to preserve and extend individual rights).
The $240,000 grant is being spread among the Southern States to bolster state Councils on Human Relations. South Carolina’s Council will receive $10,000 for the period September, 1954-Sep-tember, 1955.
Added financial help, although
on a diminishing scale, will be provided for two more years, after which the Southern Regional Council “prayerfully” hopes that the state organization will be self-supporting.
At the moment, the South Carolina organization comprises only two full-time workers; Mrs. Spearman, and Mrs. Warren Greene, office manager. They maintain a small office at 1508 Lady Street, in Columbia.
Mrs. Spearman has long been active in activities and organization which seek to promote improved and expanded inter-racial understanding and cooperation. She is a native of Marion County, and earned a master’s degree in religious education from Columbia University after attending Converse College.
The Southern Regional Council, which could be described as the parent organization of the various Councils on Human Relations (although they are independent of its control) is the successor organization to the old Commission on Inter-racial Cooperation, founded after World War I.
Harold C. Fleming, assistant director of the Southern Regional Council, which has offices in Atlanta, says this of the organization:
“In essence, the Council’s approach rests on the belief that every Southern state and most Southern communities have people of both races who can work together as equals.
“Through their efforts, we believe the South can adjust to the legal changes now required and ultimately achieve a society in which racial distinctions will be eliminated from public life.
“We see our role as that of encouraging and assisting with information and professional services the people who feel this way. We see little point in denouncing those who feel otherwise, but believe that in time many of them will come to share our views.”"

[Title]: "Article, 1955 August 10, "Racial Amity and Good Will Is S.C. Council's Mission" by W.D. Workman, Jr."
[Transcript]: "Racial Amity And Good Will Is S. C Council’s Mission
AUG 10 1955
By W. D. Workman, Jr.
A little organization with a big mission is seeking to bring South Carolinians around to the frame of mind that problems growing out of the Supreme Court’s anti-segregation decision can best be met by biracial amity on the local level.
The South Carolina Council on Human Relations has no specific answer or answers to the complex questions arising out of the segregation issue, but it does have the conviction that those answers necessarily will demand the best thought and action from responsible leaders of both races.
Along with that conviction seems to be the basic assumption that the state must move in the direction of compliance with the Supreme Court decision.
But even so, the Council is making no pronouncements of what should or should not be done. Its president, The Rev. J. Claude Evans, editor of the Methodist Advocate, describes himself as a “moderate” in the field of race relations and is frank to admit that he has no simple, sure solution to the problem growing out of the segregation decision.
He places his emphasis on the need for establishing more and better “communication” between the races, for finding out the facts involved in each local situation, and for making biracial studies of local involvements and possibilities.
The state executive director of the Council on Human Relations, Mrs. Alice N. Spearman, feels that the Council contributes more by stressing “processes” rather than panaceas.
In her constant movement a., bout South Carolina, she seeks to bring existing agencies into greater cooperation with one another on questions affecting race relations.
Logically enough, her attention is primarily concerned with the
problem of school segregation, and she is actively promoting the formation of study groups of citizens in communities where the problem is or is expected to become acute.
Only secondarily is she attempting to build up membership in the Council on Human Relations.
Actually, there are fewer than a half-dozen local councils in the entire state. Rock Hill is the most active, for it has been stimulated by an outspoken Catholic priest, the Very Rev. Maurice Shean, and enjoys a degree of official recognition in that Mayor Em-mette Jerome is a member of the state board and has appointed a Mayor’s Committee on Human Relations.,
In Anderson, the Christian Council on Human Relations is serving the same cause. In Spartanburg, the United Church Women are carrying on similar work.
Informal meeting are held elsewhere in the state, and the state Council has individual members scattered throughout South Carolina who maintain their annual $3.50 memberships or who make other contributions to the state or local work.
The South Carolina Council on Human Relations (and those of other Southern States) grew out of the Southern Regional Council.
Last year that organization, which is dedicated to “equal opportunity for all peoples in the South,” received a $240,000 grant from the Fund for the Republic.
(The Fund was established by the Ford Foundation in 1952 to preserve and extend individual rights).
The $240,000 grant is being spread among the Southern States to bolster state Councils on Human Relations. South Carolina’s Council will receive $10,000 for the period September, 1954-Sep-tember, 1955.
Added financial help, although
on a diminishing scale, will be provided for two more years, after which the Southern Regional Council “prayerfully” hopes that the state organization will be self-supporting.
At the moment, the South Carolina organization comprises only two full-time workers; Mrs. Spearman, and Mrs. Warren Greene, office manager. They maintain a small office at 1508 Lady Street, in Columbia.
Mrs. Spearman has long been active in activities and organization which seek to promote improved and expanded inter-racial understanding and cooperation. She is a native of Marion County, and earned a master’s degree in religious education from Columbia University after attending Converse College.
The Southern Regional Council, which could be described as the parent organization of the various Councils on Human Relations (although they are independent of its control) is the successor organization to the old Commission on Inter-racial Cooperation, founded after World War I.
Harold C. Fleming, assistant director of the Southern Regional Council, which has offices in Atlanta, says this of the organization:
“In essence, the Council’s approach rests on the belief that every Southern state and most Southern communities have people of both races who can work together as equals.
“Through their efforts, we be. lieve the South can adjust to the legal changes now required and ultimately achieve a society in which racial distinctions will be eliminated from public life.
“We see our role as that of encouraging and assisting with information and professional services the people who feel this way. We see little point in denouncing those who feel otherwise, but believe that in time many of them will come to share our views.”"

[Title]: "Letter, 1962 September 6, Mrs. Alice Brown to Rev. Adams to asking for rise to a salary, page 1"
[Transcript]: "1228 Heidt Street Columbia, South Carolina
September 6, 1962
Rev. E. A. Adams, Chairman
Board of the Good Samaritan Waverley Hospital
2113 Lady Street Columbia, South Carolina
Dear Mrs Chairman:
I am sure you will agree that the cost of living has doubled in the past year. With uncounted added expenses, more money is needed to meet certain obligations. For these reasons, I am asking you to raise my salary to one hundred dollars. I have been waiting to see what would happen, but I just cannot continue to be responsible for my departments if I cannot get it.
I am sure that you did not know that you have only four Registered Nurses on the staff that are not working on a full timejob. Two of them have been there less than six months. This does not speak well for the hospital because they are just working until they get tired. I am sure you know that they would not quit a job that paid more money. Mr. Chairman, Good Samaritan needs good nurses, as does any other hospital, but if the pay is poor, you will have them changing every month or every week. This is not good. We need intelligent nurses on the staff. We have just about everything a small hospital should have in the line of equipment, but if the nurses are unable to use it properly, orgive it to the doctors, we may as well not have it.
I am the only nurse that has been there over five years. I cannot do any more than I am doing to satisfy the doctors. I go out of my way to help, but more cooperation is needed. The main reasons for lack of it are poor salaries and inexperienced help. Seemingly, there is too much help in some departments and not enough in.others. Of course, this would come under the arrangements of the Chief Nurse. There is poor organization and lack of ingenuity. I am supervisor of the operating room and central supply. These departments' work has tripled since I have been there. This means that I need more help."

Dear Doctor Adams :
I am in receipt of your letter and the check for $35.00	, as expense account for the Bureau Of Research , in regards to the brief history of the Eighth Episcopal District ; covering a period of 1920 to che present .
